sentence: Sciatica is the name given to symptoms that arise when the sciatic nerve is irritated or compressed.
This nerve runs from the lower back down to the feet.
The NHS describes the symptoms as pain, tingling, numbness or weakness in one leg, which are often worse with movement, sneezing or coughing.
A medical review describes the typical picture as pain in one leg that is more severe than any back pain, often running below the knee, with tingling or numbness in the lower leg.
Versus Arthritis describes the pain as travelling from the back or buttock down the leg towards the foot.
The NHS also says that back pain on its own is not usually sciatica.
The NHS says a slipped disc is the most common cause of sciatica.
Versus Arthritis explains that in this case a disc in the back bulges and presses on a nerve, squeezing and irritating a nerve root.
A medical review likewise says sciatica is usually caused by irritation of a nerve root, most often from a herniated lumbar disc.
Other causes listed by the NHS are spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis and an injury to the back.
Spinal stenosis is a narrowing of the spaces in the spine, and spondylolisthesis is when one bone in the spine slips out of position.
note: Textbook definitions of the two terms the NHS names.

NICE also says a risk stratification tool, such as the STarT Back tool, can be considered at first contact to guide shared decisions about care.

sentence: The NHS lists exercises, painkillers and physiotherapy as the main treatments.
A medical review describes initial treatment as conservative, with education, advice to stay active and continue daily activities, and adequate pain relief.
NICE puts self-management and information about the condition at the centre of care.
Versus Arthritis notes that a physiotherapist can help recommend an exercise programme.
The NHS says paracetamol is unlikely to help and that it is unclear how much anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen help.
NICE does not recommend gabapentinoids for sciatica and advises against offering oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for it.
It also advises against opioids for chronic sciatica, and against belts or corsets, foot orthotics, traction and ultrasound.
The NHS says recovery usually takes from a few weeks to a few months, though it can take longer and sciatica may return.
The NHS suggests staying active, doing regular sciatica exercises and using heat packs on the painful area.
NHS hospital self-care advice says there is no single best exercise for sciatica, so choosing activities that a person enjoys is reasonable.
A medical review recommends continuing daily activities rather than stopping them.
For severe cases, the NHS says people may be referred for procedures such as epidural injections or decompression surgery.
Versus Arthritis says injections are sometimes used for severe sciatica when other treatments have not worked, and that an operation is sometimes needed to free the nerve.
A medical review says referral to a specialist is generally considered when symptoms do not improve after several weeks of conservative treatment.

sentence: The NHS says sciatica on both sides, worsening weakness or numbness in the leg, numbness around the genitals or bottom, and problems controlling the bladder or bowels need urgent attention.
The NHS route is an A&E visit or a call to 999, and it advises against driving yourself.
Clinical literature describes cauda equina syndrome as a rare but serious complication in which the nerve bundle at the bottom of the spinal canal is compressed.
Its features include difficulty passing urine, numbness in the saddle area around the perineum, pain in both legs, weakness, and bowel or bladder control problems.
Surgical decompression is described as the effective treatment.
A UK patient leaflet says outcomes are better especially when treatment starts within 24 hours of the symptoms beginning.
Leg pain that is not improving is a different situation, and a GP appointment is the usual route for discussing it.
note: Signposting; referral considered when symptoms persist.

What it is: Irritation or compression of the sciatic nerve, which runs from the lower back to the feet
Typical symptoms: Pain, tingling, numbness or weakness in one leg
Most common cause: A slipped disc
Usually diagnosed by: History and physical examination; scans are not routinely offered in non-specialist settings
Usual recovery: A few weeks to a few months, sometimes longer
Main treatments: Exercises, painkillers and physiotherapy; injections or surgery in severe cases
Emergency signs: Sciatica on both sides, worsening leg weakness, numbness around the genitals or bottom, bladder or bowel problems: call 999 or go to A&E
